displayQuote: Every artist was first an amateur

meta.title: Who really said "Every artist was first an amateur"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Emerson wrote it — the opening line of a passage in "Progress of Culture," Letters and Social Aims (1876). Often mis-worded "at first."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every artist was first an amateur'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Emerson — from "Progress of Culture," Letters and Social Aims (1876), though the line is often mis-worded and quoted out of context.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Emerson wrote it in “Progress of Culture,” an essay collected in Letters and Social Aims (1876). The exact sentence — “Every artist was first an amateur” — opens a passage on how skill ripens: “The ear outgrows the tongue… the hand obeys the same lesson.” The wording and source are consistently documented in sourced quotation archives.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letters and Social Aims, essay “Progress of Culture”
Widely noted as Emerson’s second Phi Beta Kappa oration, Harvard, 1867

source.excerpt: Every artist was first an amateur. The ear outgrows the tongue, is sooner ripe and perfect; but the tongue is always learning to say what the ear has taught it, and the hand obeys the same lesson.
trail: The curated archive WIST traces the line to “Progress of Culture,” Letters and Social Aims (1876).
The Quotations Page gives the identical source: Letters and Social Aims: Progress of Culture.
“Progress of Culture” is a chapter of the collection, as the Internet Archive scan of Letters and Social Aims confirms.
The full Project Gutenberg e-text of Letters and Social Aims includes “Progress of Culture” (page 183) and the line in full.
source.excerptNote: The famous line is the opening sentence of this passage; it is almost always quoted alone, detached from the point about ear, tongue and hand.

sourceLink.text: Letters and Social Aims at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: “Progress of Culture” was collected in Letters and Social Aims, first published in 1876 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — and Emerson died in 1882, so the text is firmly in the public domain.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.heading: About Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.metaLine: 1803–1882 · American essayist, poet and leader of Transcendentalism
author.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson was the central figure of American Transcendentalism, a lecturer and essayist whose addresses and collections — from Nature and “Self-Reliance” to the later Letters and Social Aims — shaped 19th-century American thought. “Progress of Culture,” where this line appears, was delivered as his second Phi Beta Kappa oration at Harvard, three decades after his celebrated 1837 address “The American Scholar.” Because he is a magnet for feel-good pseudo-quotes, it is worth stressing that this one is genuinely his.

misattribution.heading: Genuine, but often garbled
misattribution.intro: The credit to Emerson is real — the trouble is that the line is often mis-worded or cited so loosely that its true home gets lost.

items.why: An inserted ‘at’ circulates widely — e.g. this popular write-up — but Emerson’s text reads ‘was first an amateur.’
The sentence is almost always shown alone, cut off from the surrounding remark that ‘the ear outgrows the tongue’ — turning an observation about how skill matures into a bare pep-slogan.

misattribution.truthLine: It really is Emerson’s: the opening sentence of a passage in “Progress of Culture,” Letters and Social Aims, as documented by WIST and The Quotations Page.

context.heading: What he actually meant
lead: In “Progress of Culture” Emerson is less handing out encouragement than describing an order of learning: perception outruns performance. “The ear outgrows the tongue,” he writes — we can recognize excellence before we can produce it, and the hand only slowly catches up to what the ear already knows.
Read whole, ‘Every artist was first an amateur’ is not so much a promise that anyone can make it as an observation that mastery is downstream of long, humble apprenticeship.
context.pull: “The tongue is always learning to say what the ear has taught it.”
